note: Synthetic passages written for the coref host fixtures. No gold or player narration.

passages.text:
The bell over the door rings as you step into the lantern shop. Behind the counter, Odile Varga looks up from a tray of brass fittings and sets down her pliers.

"You're the one Tamsin sent," she says. "She told me you'd want the green glass."

A tall man in a salt-stained coat leans against the shelf of unlit wicks. He doesn't turn around, but his reflection in the window watches you. Odile follows your gaze and frowns at him.

"Ignore Brannock. He's been here since noon and hasn't bought a thing."

Brannock finally faces you. "I'm waiting for the tide," he says. "The courier who carries my letters won't sail until it turns."

Odile snorts and goes back to her fittings. She hums while she works, and the tune is one your mother used to sing.

Rain hammers the roof of the old mill. The two sisters sit on either side of the cold stove, and neither of them speaks for a long time.

The elder sister, Maren, finally breaks the silence. "You should have told me about the debt." Her voice is quiet, but her hands are shaking.

The younger one, Liesl, pulls her shawl tighter. She stares at the floorboards. "I thought I could pay it before you found out."

Maren stands and paces to the window. She watches the road, where a rider in a gray cloak waits under the dripping oaks. "He's been there since dawn," she says. "The collector won't leave until he has something."

Liesl joins her sister at the glass. The rider lifts his hood, and both women go still when they see his face.

The ferry  creaks against the pier—its ropes groan… and the captain, a half-elf named Corwin Dusk, waves you aboard.


“Mind the gap,” he says. “Last week a merchant’s mule fell in. Poor thing didn’t make it, and neither did his cheese.”

His first mate, Pell, laughs—a short, sharp bark. She’s coiling rope on the foredeck, and she doesn’t look up. “Don’t listen to him. The mule swam to shore. It’s fatter than ever.”

Corwin shrugs. “I’m not paid to tell the truth, I’m paid to steer.”

The caravan leaves the walled city at first light, and by midmorning the towers are only a smudge behind you. Wagons creak in a long line over the dry road. At the head of the column rides Captain Ysolde Harrow, a broad woman with a scar through one eyebrow and a habit of counting the wagons twice an hour.

She drops back to ride beside you when the sun is high. "You're the scribe," she says. "The guild told me you'd keep the ledgers and stay out of trouble. Can you do both?"

You tell her you can. She looks unconvinced, but she nods and points with her chin toward the third wagon. A boy of perhaps twelve sits on its tailboard, swinging his legs and whittling a stick into nothing.

"That's Fenn," she says. "His father owns half the cargo. If he falls off, it's my neck. If he wanders off, it's yours."

Fenn hears his name and grins at you. He holds up the stick, which looks a little like a horse if you squint, and then goes back to carving.

By afternoon the road climbs into the hills. The drovers curse at the oxen, and the oxen ignore them. Ysolde rides up and down the line, shouting at the slow wagons and checking the straps on the fast ones. When a wheel cracks on a stone, she is off her horse before the wagon stops, and she has the spare wheel half on before the drover has finished swearing.

At dusk the caravan circles in a meadow beside a stream. The cooks light their fires. Fenn appears at your elbow with a bowl of stew he did not pay for and asks if scribes ever get to fight bandits.

"Sometimes," says a voice behind you. It is the old guard, Tobin, who has said nothing all day. He settles onto a log with a groan and lays his crossbow across his knees. "Mostly they write down who died."

Fenn's face falls. Tobin laughs, a dry wheeze, and tells the boy he was joking. Then he looks at you, and you are not sure that he was.

Later, when the fires burn low, Ysolde walks the circle one last time. She stops beside your bedroll and crouches. "Tobin likes you," she says quietly. "He doesn't like anyone. Keep an eye on the boy tonight. Something has been following us since the ford, and I want to know what it is before it decides to introduce itself."

She rises and walks away before you can answer. Across the meadow, Fenn is already asleep under the third wagon, one hand still curled around his carved horse. Beyond the firelight, something moves in the tall grass, and then it is still again.

You do not sleep much. Near midnight Tobin relieves the first watch, and you hear him humming an old marching song under his breath. The stream chatters over its stones. Somewhere far off an owl calls twice and falls silent, and the horses shift and stamp in their lines as if they smell something the people cannot.
